captions.text: This bright, you'd take me for a copy.
I'm not. King Goujian of Yue used me.
Dug from a tomb in nineteen sixty-five.
Two thousand five hundred years, still sharp.

facts.text: The Sword of Goujian Special Exhibition is on the second floor of the South Hall and covers 600 m².
The sword is a national-treasure-level relic.
The sword is one of the Hubei Provincial Museum's four most treasured pieces.
The exhibition is built around the sword and has three sections: 'Annals of the Yue State', 'Astonishing Discovery' and 'King of Swords'.
The museum's display uses Yue history to tell the story of the marriage alliance between King Zhao of Chu and King Goujian of Yue.
The museum presents the sword's technical achievements through 'the mystery of its imperishability'.
The sword is a tin-bronze sword from the end of the Spring and Autumn period.
The sword was used by King Goujian of Yue.
The sword was excavated in December 1965 from Chu Tomb No. 1 at Wangshan, Jiangling County, Hubei.
The sword has been held by the Hubei Provincial Museum since after National Day 1999.
The sword is on the third list of relics forbidden to be exhibited abroad, issued in 2013.
China Daily gives the sword as 56 centimeters long and 5 centimeters wide.
The sword is in the Hubei Provincial Museum's permanent collection.
The sword dates back 2,500 years.
China Daily describes it as a 'shining and rust-free bronze sword'.
China Daily says the hegemon Goujian used this sword to annex his rivals' territory after twenty years of humiliation.
Goujian reigned 496-465 BC.
The sword is 55.6 cm long, including an 8.4 cm hilt.
The blade is 4.6 cm wide at its base.
The sword weighs 875 grams.
The sword still has a sharp blade and shows no tarnish.
It has been speculated that the sword's chemical composition, together with the almost air-tight scabbard, likely explains its preservation.
The sword's edges contain more tin, which makes them harder and better at holding a sharp edge.
Sulfur reduces the chance of tarnish in the sword's patterns.
Wikipedia says that in 1994, while the sword was on loan to Singapore, a worker accidentally bumped it against the case and left a 7-millimetre crack.
Wikipedia says the sword likely also had its own name, as other swords of Goujian's did, but that name has been lost.
The Sword of Goujian Special Exhibition draws millions of Chinese and foreign visitors every year.
